summary: Extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) so a client can ask a path computation server to work out routes for point-to-multipoint traffic engineering label switched paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It was replaced by RFC 8306.

eli5.summary: One road to one place is easy to plan, but a delivery tree that branches to many places is harder. This lets a router ask a helper computer to plan that branching route.

questions: how to compute p2mp te lsp paths
how does pcep support point-to-multipoint paths
what is p2mp TE in MPLS
how do you compute a delivery tree with PCEP
subtitle: Enabling path computations for delivery trees instead of single paths

tldr.problem: The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture allows network servers to compute optimal routes. However, the original PCEP protocol was designed only for point-to-point paths. Delivery trees that branch to multiple destinations need different computation logic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6006 adds PCEP extensions including new message flags, tree-aware endpoint objects, objective functions for tree optimization (shortest path tree, minimum cost tree), and mechanisms to fragment large requests across multiple messages.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now automatically compute and optimize point-to-multipoint traffic engineering paths in MPLS and GMPLS. RFC 8306 replaced this RFC in 2018 with consolidated rules.

today: RFC 8306 replaced RFC 6006 in December 2018. It is the current standard for PCEP P2MP extensions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) is a network component that computes optimal paths through the network according to constraints and objectives. The original PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) in RFC 5440 handles point-to-point (P2P) path requests: one source, one destination.

RFC 6006 extends PCEP to support point-to-multipoint (P2MP) paths, where a single source sends data to multiple destinations along a tree structure. This is essential for applications like video conferencing, IPTV delivery, and disaster recovery networks. P2MP paths are defined in RFC 4875 for MPLS-TE and GMPLS, and RFC 6006 provides the protocol extensions to request and receive P2MP path computations from a PCE.
sections.eli5: A PCE is a helper that plans good routes through a network. This RFC teaches it how to plan delivery trees that go from one place to many places.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions for P2MP Requests
sections.content:
RFC 6006 adds new flags to the PCEP Request Parameters (RP) object. The P2MP flag (N-bit) indicates whether a request is for a P2MP path. The Fragmentation flag (F-bit) tells the receiver that a large request is split across multiple messages, identified by the same request ID. The ERO-compression flag (E-bit) indicates whether routes are returned in compressed form (one primary route plus branches) rather than expanded form.

The END-POINTS object is extended to list multiple destinations efficiently and to distinguish four types of leaves: new leaves to add, old leaves to remove, old leaves that can be reoptimized, and old leaves that must not change. This enables a single request to add, remove, or modify parts of an existing tree. The protocol also defines new objective functions: Shortest Path Tree (SPT) minimizes the maximum hop cost, while Minimum Cost Tree (MCT) minimizes total link costs.
sections.eli5: The protocol adds flags that say 'this is a many-destination request', 'this request is part of a bigger message', and 'show me the tree layout'. It also lets you say which destinations are new, which to remove, and which to keep.

sections.title: Tree Operations: Adding, Removing, and Reoptimizing
sections.content:
RFC 6006 specifies how to request modifications to existing P2MP trees. To add new leaves, the PCC sends END-POINTS with leaf type 1. To remove leaves, it sends leaf type 2, and the PCE must report an error if it cannot prune. To reoptimize an existing tree, leaf types 3 and 4 specify which leaves can be modified and which must stay fixed.

When adding or removing leaves, the PCC provides the existing tree's route (Record Route Object or RRO list) so the PCE can optimize the combined tree. The RFC includes nine examples showing combinations like adding leaves with full reoptimization, partial reoptimization, or no reoptimization. Large trees are handled by request and response fragmentation: if a tree has hundreds of leaves, the request splits into multiple PCEP messages, each marked with an F-bit.
sections.eli5: You can tell the PCE 'add these places to my tree', 'remove those places', or 'make these places faster but keep those the same'. If the tree is huge, the message splits into chunks.

sections.title: Message Format and Synchronization
sections.content:
P2MP requests use secondary route objects: the Secondary Explicit Route Object (SERO) encodes each source-to-leaf sub-path, and the Secondary Record Route Object (SRRO) records the actual route taken. A reply message pairs END-POINTS (to identify which leaves are added, removed, or unchanged) with paths.

RFC 6006 also extends the SVEC (Synchronization VECtor) object to handle cases where multiple P2MP trees must be computed together and their paths must be diverse. New SVEC flags request partial path diversity for specific leaves and link-direction diversity. When a leaf is unreachable, the PCE can return an UNREACH-DESTINATION object listing which destinations failed. Branch Node Capability objects let the PCC specify which routers can act as branch points in the tree.
sections.eli5: The response message says which destinations got new routes, which kept the old ones, and which could not be reached. You can ask for multiple trees that avoid using the same links.

sections.title: Error Handling and Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
PCEs advertise P2MP support via a new TLV in the PCEP OPEN message or via OSPF and IS-IS discovery (RFC 5088, RFC 5089). If a PCE receives a P2MP request but does not support P2MP, it MUST return an error (Error-Type 16, Value 2). New error types cover insufficient memory, inconsistent END-POINTS, missing leaf types, and fragmented request failure.

The RFC defines metric types specific to P2MP: P2MP IGP metric, P2MP TE metric, and P2MP hop count metric, which sum the costs across all links in the tree. These allow the PCE to optimize the overall tree cost rather than per-destination cost.
sections.eli5: If the PCE cannot handle P2MP requests or runs out of memory, it says so. You can ask it to minimize different kinds of costs, like total hops or total link load.
